blocks.content: About 59 percent of the land area of India is liable to seismic hazard damage of moderate to very high intensity.

rows: Deccan Plateau, parts of Rajasthan, Karnataka, Madhya Pradesh
Kerala, Goa, Lakshadweep, parts of Uttar Pradesh, Maharashtra
Delhi-NCR, Jammu & Kashmir, Sikkim, Northern Bihar, parts of Maharashtra
North-East India, Uttarakhand, Himachal Pradesh, Rann of Kutch, A&N Islands

items: Zone I is no longer used in the official BIS seismic map; Zone II is now the lowest risk zone.
Delhi-NCR falls under Zone IV (High Damage Risk Zone), while the entire North-Eastern region lies in Zone V.
The Bureau of Indian Standards (BIS) code IS 1893 is the official standard for earthquake-resistant design of structures.

blocks.title: Key Takeaways
items: India is categorized into four seismic hazard zones by the Bureau of Indian Standards (BIS): Zone II, III, IV, and V.
Zone I was phased out and merged into Zone II in the updated IS 1893 seismic code.
Nearly 59% of India's total landmass is vulnerable to moderate to severe earthquake hazard.
Zone V represents the highest risk area, encompassing North-East India, the Himalayan belt, Rann of Kutch, and Andaman & Nicobar Islands.
Seismic intensity is mapped using the Modified Mercalli Intensity (MMI) scale alongside the Medvedev-Sponheuer-Karnik (MSK) scale.
